text: These Care Advisors will also be deployed at SSG career fairs held at the various M3@Towns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The aim is to increase awareness within the community about the activities and services offered by SSG, as well as share information on Future Ready programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The community can look out for our Care Advisors at the employment fairs, to get the necessary advice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: MENDAKI will also join forces with NTUC to help our Malay workers secure job placements in emerging and growth sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: More details on the Tunas Bersama M3 programme will be shared in the near future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: (In English): Mr Chairman, the community has shown good progress in employment in the last 10 years and we aim to do even better in the years to come.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Our growth has only been possible with the strong support of our community and our partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, let us all work together as one, keeping the community at the heart of what we are doing so that they, too, can do well for themselves and contribute back to society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This continuous cycle of support would go a long way in strengthening the competencies of our Community of Success.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: (In Malay):   Our asatizahs are well-regarded within the community for their important role.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In fact, there had been prominent religious scholars in Singapore, such as Ustaz Syed Ahmad Semait, Ustaz Syed Abdillah al-Jufri and Ustaz Ahmad Sonhadji.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They have made significant contributions to the Islamic religious discourse in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The religious texts they produced are still being read and used as reference today.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many of my peers grew up with Ustaz Ahmad Sonhadji's foundation text – Mari Sembahyang, or "Let's Pray".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are fortunate to have our own local madrasahs that ensure a steady pipeline of asatizah talents.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They are also familiar with our way of life within Singapore's context.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Since the curriculum review implemented over 20 years ago, madrasah students now are capable of pursuing either Islamic Studies at the higher education level or take up secular education.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Abdul Samad asked about the retention rate of students in the madrasah system.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Among those who remain, about half will pursue post-secondary education in secular institutions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Based on the Asatizah Manpower Planning Study, this is almost sufficient.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, we should be proud that our madrasah students have no problems switching to secular education.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: However, it should be emphasised that the main goal of madrasah education here is to produce new asatizahs who can guide the Singapore Muslim community and expand our asatizah sector, in addition to contributing to broader sectors should they wish to do so.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For students who eventually become asatizahs, they need to be able to provide sound religious advice.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They need to understand the lived realities of the community here and be sensitive to the cultural nuances to guide the Muslim community in navigating new and complex challenges.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In line with this year's focus on enhancing competencies within our community, we will support the asatizah sector to acquire impactful competencies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: First, we want to develop critical bodies of knowledge for the asatizahs, so that they can be exposed to broader perspectives and worldviews.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Second, we will enhance the career pathways for the religious sector, to ensure that this profession remains appealing and relevant.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Third, we want to mobilise community resources to sustain the development of our religious sector.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has illustrated the need for our asatizahs to be prepared to address complex issues in a contemporary society and unprecedented global challenges.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In addition to acquiring a deep knowledge of our religious traditions and having a strong character, our asatizahs must also possess the competency to contextualise religious teachings to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This requires them to form a strong connection with our multiracial society, in order to better understand our experience of living in a country full of diversity.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is especially so, because our experience as a Muslim-minority community is different from those of Muslim-majority societies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Therefore, I agree with Dr Wan Rizal that we need to develop bodies of knowledge that can guide Muslim-minority communities living in multi-religious societies to navigate contemporary socio-religious issues more confidently, while enabling them to practise their faith with ease.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Abdul Samad asked about efforts to help returning Islamic Studies graduates contextualise their knowledge for the local community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is the aim of the PCICS, which provides returning students with the framework to apply their knowledge to the local context.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: One of the graduates who benefited from the PCICS programme is Ustazah Sarah El Rani.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: She found the programme useful in deepening her understanding of Islamic traditions, such as the use of Maqasid Shariah in Islamic Jurisprudence to address new challenges faced by societies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This allowed her to better understand its application in the Singapore context, such as the adjustments made to religious practices as part of COVID-19 preventive measures.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To address Dr Shahira Abdullah's query on support given to returning Islamic Studies graduates, our key focus is to ensure that these graduates contribute back to the Muslim religious sector in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The PCICS equips them with the knowledge to provide progressive religious guidance, while exposing them to critical skills and competencies that can also be applied in relevant non-religious sectors.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: MUIS will be organising the International Conference on Communities of Success (ICCOS) later this year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Dr Wan Rizal asked about the key objectives of this conference and how it will benefit the Singapore Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Building on the two pre-conference seminars held last year, the upcoming conference will bring together religious scholars to develop critical bodies of knowledge that can guide Muslim-minority communities in multicultural societies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: With the theme "Contributing Citizens, Dynamic Institutions", it will focus on how enlightened and contextualised religious guidance, coupled with institutional support, can empower Muslims to live as dignified citizens and contribute to the nation's development.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Delegates from various nations will be invited to share and learn from one another.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For students who have done well in the madrasahs, I hope more of you will go into the religious sector and see the asatizah profession not merely as an employment opportunity, but as a meaningful and attractive calling.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is my hope for students who have done well in the "A" Levels, the IB Diploma, as well as the Aliyah programmes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They are excellent candidates for the next generation of our future asatizahs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will continue to support these students in their education, including providing prestigious scholarships for the talented ones to further their studies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is how we can ensure strong leadership renewal in our religious institutions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For those that show potential, MUIS offers the Religious Leadership and Talent Development Programme, or RLTD.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It provides participants opportunities to have fireside chats with community and religious figures and benefit from mentoring programmes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Most participants have found the programmes useful as part of their career development in the religious sector.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This addresses the questions from Dr Wan Rizal and Mr Mohd Fahmi Bin Aliman about plans to develop and groom asatizah leadership in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Under the RLTD as well, MUIS is introducing the Leadership Milestone Programme which provides formal training for asatizahs with good potential.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The objective is to further develop and groom them for future leadership roles.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: First is the general leadership track, where asatizahs will benefit from a wide range of courses offered by various public and private institutions, to hone their competencies before they lead an organisation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This includes courses in financial management, strategy formulation and human capital management.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This seeks to deepen the asatizah's knowledge and appreciation of our religious traditions and its application in the Singapore context.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Under this track, the Leadership Executive Programme will provide a platform for asatizahs to have discussions on the religious life of the Singapore Muslim community and gain a deeper understanding of policy issues.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These initiatives will expose our asatizahs to a wide range of issues, to help nurture their leadership potential and hone their critical thinking, especially on religious issues impacting our Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Ultimately, our aim is to prepare the younger generation of asatizahs to be ready to serve when called to higher office, including helming our key religious institutions, such as the Mufti, the President of the Syariah Court and the Kadi at ROMM.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Therefore, we need to structure clear and meaningful career pathways for the asatizah.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This includes remuneration for the asatizahs, as asked by Mr Abdul Samad and Dr Shahira Abdullah.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will need to ensure the sector is equally attractive as competing sectors.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Details will be provided when the review is completed.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will also need to fund the long-term needs of our religious sector.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is why there are plans to encourage the wakaf culture within our community, as asked by Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Dr Shahira Abdullah.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Since the launch of Singapore Community Wakaf, an Advisory Panel has been formed to get feedback from key stakeholders and put forth recommendations on how to galvanise community support in the implementation of this wakaf.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This year, MUIS formed working groups, comprising MUIS officers and industry experts, to implement detailed action plans for the Singapore Community Wakaf.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It will take into consideration the recommendations of the Advisory Panel Report that was submitted last year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This includes plans like engaging our institutions like the wakaf and mosques to pool our assets together and invest their reserves to grow the corpus fund; and second, encouraging the community's participation through public education initiatives on wakaf, particularly on wealth and legacy planning.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Initiatives, such as the RLTD, PCICS and the International Conference on Communities of Success (ICCOS), are key enablers to propel the asatizah sector forward and we will need the community's support to achieve its desired outcomes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Singapore Community Wakaf will thus be crucial in catering for the long-term needs of the Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Chairman, in conclusion, my colleagues and I have spoken on three strategies to strengthen our competencies as a Community of Success.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Underpinning these strategies are strong and resilient families who provide a conducive environment for children to grow and achieve their fullest potential.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Here, our community partners and institutions play an important role.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our Naib Kadis, for example, are key partners in supporting the work of building strong and resilient Muslim families, especially through the Bersamamu programme.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In this regard, we will journey with our community every step of the way to propel them towards success.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Chairman, I would like to thank Minister Masagos Zulkifli, Second Minister Mohamad Maliki and Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad for answering my questions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: First is in regard to the GIC-MENDAKI scholarship for Singaporean students, I really welcome the announcement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is a good step in that direction.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I need to seek further details on the scholarship.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How many recipients will be awarded the scholarship?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: And would there be further expansion to possibly postgraduate scholarships because I mentioned that the SkillsFuture credit take-up is quite low.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, the lifelong learning efforts in the community can be enhanced even further through postgraduate scholarships as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: My second clarification is with regard to the question in my cut.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What are our plans for a sectoral-based approach to enhance our PMET representations in sectors which are growing as well as sectors that are growth industries as it is now?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Do keep watch for this because I am quite sure it will excite quite a number of prospective young graduates who are keen to join the financial sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On postgraduate scholarships, generally, as a basis, if you look at where the Government is putting its resources today, we have made a lot of push with SkillsFuture to support individuals, regardless of where they are, to gain mastery of skills and master lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is not just about going for a Master's or postgraduate degree, but there are also other skills training and certificates you can go for postgraduate studies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But even today, there are schemes like the SkillsFuture Mid-career Enhanced subsidy and the SkillsFuture Work-Study degree.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: You can also go for the Work-Study degree that is open to all eligible Singaporeans, including the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These are already available scholarships that are provided across nationally.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There is a certain trend that we are going to work towards to look for more like-minded corporate partners who could support the move of our Malay community.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: One, to enhance and to provide them with a pathway into growth sectors, but also more importantly for them, it also helps to build diversity and a strong Singaporean Core for PMETs in the various companies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We hope to announce more in future, but it is going to be hard work in the next coming months and years to make sure that we can expand this programme further.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: I think the bigger issue will be the general estate planning, future planning and retirement security of our community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: So, I agree that public awareness is key.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: If I may ask, with the workgroup, will there be other efforts to be made to approach the community and engage the community through the community partners, preferably through M3 and other Malay/Muslim organisations to tailor-make the message, for example, just like "Dadah Itu Haram" campaign that is quite effective for the community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This could also include legislative amendments and the proposals that I suggested in terms of the Syariah court and MUIS' recommendations.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For Wakaf Masyarakat Singapura (WMS), like the Member has pointed out, the last one was given almost 40 years ago.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Unfortunately, I would say there are some constraints on how the benefits of such bequeathed properties and trusts should be distributed.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Sometimes, we have problems finding the village in a country that does not exist anymore or people whom we do not know whether they are still around to benefit from these assets and trusts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And, therefore, going forward, we have to look at how these problems do not get encountered again by us and future generations.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I also want to point out that in formulating WMS, it is beyond just calling the community to bequeath their assets; it is also calling them to prepare their children to be well-endowed through education, career and also to build their own wealth, so that they do not rely on their parents' wealth to live on in their life.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And that their parents also do not feel guilty in giving away that wealth for the sake of the community, for the future of the community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are in a good place and time right now, because, as Members have heard from many of our speeches just now, the community is at that inflexion point of being better and acquiring wealth for themselves.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: From what I see from the news recently, they were given a salary incentive of $100, but it was only offered to those working in mosques and madrasahs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I call upon the other sectors to do the same – recognise our asatizahs, give them a meaningful salary scale, salary level, let them live a dignified life like everybody else, like the ones that we want for our own children.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I believe our community is very, very generous.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have not pulled ourselves back whenever we call for support for our friends in Palestine when some calamity has befallen them.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In fact, in many circumstances, through the Rahmatan Lil Alamin Foundation (RLAF), when disasters happened around our area, we have been able to collect donations to help victims who are not Muslims, who do not live in Muslim countries.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, we have also given, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: (In Malay):   I would like to come back to my two questions on FITRAH, that is, if M3 will collaborate with the Malay/Muslim organisations, ComLink and other agencies.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Are there plans to offer and coordinate support to the family of offenders, not just at the beginning or the end of their incarceration period, but throughout the sentence so that the offender's family can emerge stronger?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Second, as the FITRAH programme requires the commitment and support from a rather large number of volunteers, how will the FITRAH structure be strengthened for the long term?

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: When we work with families, like those under FITRAH, it is very complex.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: The structure of the families is very complex.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Sometimes, you do have the father in prison, single mothers having to deal with very young children.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Sometimes, you have both parents who are in prison, incarcerated and the children are under the care of grandparents, making it very complex.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: When we started FITRAH, it was really looking at many different dimensions.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: One is to ensure that the needs of the children are supported primarily by family members who are outside, because it is the stability of the children, while the parents are incarcerated, that is very critical.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: And stability comes in the form of ensuring that they continue to be able to go to school, they are able to get support for their socio-emotional development and everything around that concept.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: And that is the first part of looking after the children – to understand their socio-emotional needs, and even their economic needs.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: At the same time, we ensure that work with the inmates continue.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: And the reason why we put the framework in place is to give a very strong message to the inmates that it is a time for reflection and rehabilitation for you, too, so that when you do come out and get released, that you do make every attempt to turn over a new leaf.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: And this is very important because, sometimes, we do come across inmates who repeat the offences and they go back in and we want to make sure that FITRAH provides comprehensive support to prevent relapses among the inmates.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Yet, at the same time, we work towards independence and self-reliance moving forward for the incarcerated individual and their families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Chairman, community harmony is important to engender a sense of collective and shared destiny.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But this can be undermined at times by misunderstandings and disputes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During our constituency work, we would have come across a range of community disputes – noise from neighbours, noise from groups playing at the basketball court downstairs, cigarette smell, incessant high-rise littering, irresponsible feeding, encroachment of common space and the list goes on.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In these disputes, one party may be puzzled about why does the other party not understand or comply with the implicit and explicit "rules"; the other party may think that there was nothing wrong with the behaviour and wonder why the complainant is making life difficult.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Small disagreements, if left unresolved, can fester into ill-feelings and anti-social behaviours with long-lasting effects.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our community is diverse, with people of different backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The idea of co-existence is important, though a delicate balance to strike.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Community norms, therefore, play a critical role in keeping a certain order and harmony in the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As time passes or as environment changes, norms could shift.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The pandemic has forced us to stay home more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We face one another more and things that used to not bother us can become difficult to bear.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, we need to review, re-establish and/or revise the norms needed in the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To do so, we need more dialogues and engagements but, most importantly, is that the community must come to a common understanding on the priorities and acceptable behaviours within the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask how MCCY will continue to enhance the framework to effectively manage community disputes and relations, while partnering Singaporeans to co-create and establish community norms in their own neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, one major lifestyle change arising from COVID-19 has been about more residents working or learning from home.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Along with this trend, we are seeing a rise in the number of disputes within the community.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: When community disputes arise, grassroots volunteers and on-the-ground agencies, such as HDB, Town Council or Police, are often the first responders to help engage the parties.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Those of us who have helped to mediate a dispute will know that they are never easy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: With the number of conflicts between neighbours on the rise, our first responders will be strained with more cases.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given this, can the Minister share if MCCY will dedicate more resources, such as improving training for our first responders, to help our communities be more effective in managing such conflicts?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Community Mediation Centre (CMC) also plays an integral role in resolving neighbour disputes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Mediation at the CMC is an informal and voluntary process, conducted by professionally-trained mediators who are volunteers from all walks of life.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Cases referred to the CMC have seen relative success.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, a legal avenue for resolving disputes is the CDRT.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The process may, therefore, result in more friction and deteriorate relationships further.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, it is important to ensure that parties engaging in the legal process will be able to ensure quick and effective justice at a lower cost.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Experts and businesses have said that this hybrid model of working and learning from home is here to stay, even if the pandemic ends.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to the Minister's plans on how the Government can strengthen existing solutions to counter the growth in community disputes, so as to preserve our social cohesion and harmony.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister share who the members of the interagency committee conducting this review are and when the review will be completed?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How many mediators does the Community Mediation Centre (CMC) currently have and is this sufficient to manage their workload?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have met residents who have a vexing dispute with their neighbours but are unwilling to let me refer them for mediation because they know their neighbour will not turn up for the session.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To improve the take-up rate of mediation, could the Ministry consider these suggestions?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, if the dispute eventually goes to the Community Dispute Resolution Tribunal (CDRT), can the Tribunal be allowed to draw an adverse inference from their non-attendance?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This potential penalty should be made clear to respondents when the invitation to the CMC is served.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, I have received feedback from residents about the difficulty they face in filing CDRT evidence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, they need to save their audio or video recordings on a CD-ROM or DVD.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most people nowadays do not have a CD-ROM burner in their home.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unfortunately, a significant number take a long time to resolve due to the uncooperative neighbours, some of whom are openly and persistently flouting the law.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These cases include harassment, obstruction of passageways, dangerous placement of objects, fire hazard and noise pollution.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry consider setting up a dedicated team for mediation and enforcement and a hotline for residents to contact for issues relating to neighbour disputes?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many residents, community partners, religious organisations, private companies and strangers reached out to me and my community to volunteer and offer various forms of help, especially to the hawkers and the vulnerable in my division.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It was very heartwarming and the community became even more closely-knit and resilient.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the pandemic placing restrictions on community events, which we used to organise in the past, we need to reorganise how we connect and strengthen ties among our neighbours.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Building friendship and trust among our neighbours must still continue to be the focus.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What we observe sometimes is that relationships become so bad that neighbours do not talk to each other and, in some cases, even dragging in other neighbours into the dispute, creating a non-harmonious living environment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that MCCY can empower our grassroots volunteers and staff with relevant skillsets to mediate disputes between neighbours.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is best when things can be settled and nipped in the bud at the local level without further straining relationships.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How will MCCY empower our grassroots leaders and staff to build on this spirit of care and continue to strengthen community life at the local neighbourhood level?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The mission of our Inter-racial and Religious Confidence Circles (IRCCs) is ever more important today as we face sharper fault lines and greater challenges to our racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When there is conflict, especially when it involves potentially sensitive racial or religious issues, we must quickly seek to resolve and nip the problem in the bud.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should not ignore it and hope for it to blow over, thereby allowing the problem to fester and blow up into a bigger problem.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The best way, really, is through mediation, with trained personnel who have the necessary knowledge and skillsets for the problem at hand.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With a mediator, whom all stakeholders can acknowledge and respect, the chances of resolving the problem is much higher.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry elaborate on how it will bring disputing parties together to resolve such issues?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must also educate our people about the customs of different races and religions, so that we can be more mindful and avoid potentially offensive behaviour.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must be respectful of one another's differences and widen the common space.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are often complaints of noise disturbances or certain practices of religious or cultural events and festivities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we approach the 20th anniversary of IRCCs in 2022, what are MCCY's plans to ensure that our IRCCs remain relevant and effective in maintaining racial and religious harmony and strengthening our social cohesion?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As a result, we are in a much stronger position today even as we ride out the current Omicron wave and look forward to a better future.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I was reminded of it recently during the Tampines East Edusave Ceremony when this lady said "Hi Miss Cheng, we finally meet".

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It turns out that she is the chairlady of her company's CSR and she had mobilised the team to help out in our mask-making during the circuit breaker.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We had only corresponded via emails and phone.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I remembered then, Standard Chartered Bank also listed my email on their CSR portal and I would get dozens of emails daily asking "How can I help?" The logistics company, taxi driver and fabric supplier who helped, all declined payment.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It was their way of contributing to fight the pandemic.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many would have also heard of neighbours helping one another with grocery purchase, mask and sanitiser collection, especially for their elderly neighbours.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our cohesiveness as a nation has strengthened over the pandemic years.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Chairman, this cohesiveness among our people and the trust in the Government that we have in Singapore are precious.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In many other parts of the world, we have seen how the pandemic had aggravated existing fault lines and even created tensions between the government and people, with anti-vaccination and anti-mask protests.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: These tensions made it more challenging to deal with the pandemic.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry share how we can continue to build upon this spirit of care and strengthen community cohesiveness in Singapore?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How can we make volunteerism and care a part of our lives and match like-minded people to the causes that they are interested in?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We are all aware of how racial riots rocked Singapore in the 1960s.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Although many years have gone by, that period holds important lessons for us.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: From time to time, racist incidents happen and we are reminded that building a multiracial and multi-religious society is, indeed, a work in progress.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Take, for example, last year, there was a viral video showing a confrontation between a man and an inter-racial couple.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We may not have the full facts of what happened, but many of us were rightly disturbed and worried after watching it.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We must never waver in our commitment to promote harmony among our people.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Therefore, the role of our IRCCs is even more important.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When I was a young volunteer, I remember IRCCs organising excursions to Hindu temples, churches and we had buka puasa over nasi dulang in mosques and got to know one another's religion better.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Unfortunately, IRCCs stopped having these programmes years ago.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What are MCCY's plans to ensure the relevance of IRCCs and its role in strengthening our social cohesion?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: Last year, we heard about anecdotes where racial remarks were made against Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: For instance, an ex-Ngee Ann Polytechnic lecturer made unwelcomed remarks about an interracial couple last year, triggering a slew of responses from the public.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: The occurrence of such incidents has thus reminded us of the need to show the greatest tolerance and respect for one another.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: MCCY has also stepped up its efforts to tackle racism and racial discrimination in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: In response to several Parliamentary Questions raised last year, MCCY mentioned it adopts a multi-pronged approach in combating racism and racial discrimination.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: MCCY's approach mainly constitutes enforcement and legal framework, encouraging respectful online behaviour, encouraging conversations on the topics of race and religion as well as enlarging the common spaces.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: These four elements of MCCY's approach would be essential in ensuring that Singapore society remains resilient and cohesive as we transition to a post-pandemic future.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: Given MCCY's efforts in promoting social harmony in Singapore, can it provide an update on efforts to continue rallying Singaporeans to step up on integration efforts and build a more cohesive society?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: Moreover, can MCCY elaborate on its upcoming plans to step up on our social cohesion efforts and partner Singaporeans to bridge existing societal fault lines?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: On the other hand, the survey also showed that online giving rose during the COVID-19 pandemic, despite an overall decline in volunteerism.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: In light of these findings, could MCCY share how it plans to leverage the growth of online volunteerism and provide more opportunities for Singaporeans to step forward?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: Moreover, could MCCY also elaborate on its efforts to reframe the public's impression of volunteerism, often associated with labour-intensive work and perceived as separate from one's social or professional lives.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: Are there online efforts to make volunteerism and care a part of the Singaporean way of life?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: Could MCCY also share its plans to provide opportunities for Singaporeans to serve others using their skills and talent and galvanise like-minded people to work together on social and community causes that interest them?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: We should engage and encourage them to participate and contribute actively to matters of national concern that will impact our society in the long run.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Over the years, MCCY has announced numerous initiatives, such as the Youth Action Challenge and digital engagements, to engage our youth and seek their views.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Mark Chay, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: There are also Conversations on Singapore Women's Development and OnePeople.sg.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Creating these platforms is commendable and well-intentioned, with the goal of bringing Singaporeans to work with one another for a better future.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Feedback is critical for growth and I would like to request that MCCY provide an update on the progress of these conversations.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I am aware that these discussions typically span a wide range of topics, such as national identity, care for the elderly, technology, governance and so on.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The impact of these dialogues would provide reliable insights into the state and progress of our nation in different areas.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, important that MCCY answers the following questions.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The world is changing in so many ways.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: What we do for entertainment today will be replaced by emerging ideas and innovations.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The future of entertainment is firmly rooted in digitisation and technology.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Netflix, for instance, has revolutionised the entertainment industry by giving customers original and high-quality on-demand content available to people regardless of location.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Other platforms, such as Twitch and YouTube, take live content to hundreds of millions of viewers around the world.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: On the future of entertainment, I would like to discuss two points: first, the need for enabling technology and the metaverse; and second, the importance of adapting to hybrid and digital events.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This will serve as the future for many things we are currently doing today.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Non-fungible tokens (NFTs), e-commerce and the integration of collectibles give the audience ownership of their fan experience.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: These will enhance interactions between users and their favourite teams.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It would be highly beneficial to Singapore if the Ministry could encourage digital content and technologies to facilitate interaction between the real and virtual worlds.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I would like the Ministry to consider a gaming, technology and digital content hub.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This hub can bring Singapore significant economic opportunities, be an incubator for human capital development and, most importantly, a gateway to youths and community engagement.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I am now moving on to my next point, the need to adapt to hybrid and digital events.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore opens post-COVID-19, rather than making digital versions of traditional physical experiences, events need to leverage digital and hybrid extensions to engage audiences better.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore needs to encourage the arts and sports sectors to adapt.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In the sports and arts industry, COVID-19 testing and safe management measures (SMMs) will remain for the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I want to encourage the Ministry to work together with event organisers and venues to ensure the safety of participants and spectators.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We must also keep in mind the viability and sustainability of such events to create practical SMMs that make sense to everyone involved.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Inclusivity and accessibility must be at the forefront of these experiences.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We must be proactive in designing and producing content that recognises and considers essential demographics.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Gender, age, sexual orientation, ethnicity, language, religion, physical and mental abilities and socio-economic status are important parameters that we must not neglect.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We want a future filled with opportunities and security for our families.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Sports and the arts are, arguably, the two most universal and influential languages we have.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I seek clarity on how the Ministry intends to encourage and promote diverse participation in sports and the arts.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Here, in Singapore, we are very fortunate to enjoy widespread access to arts and heritage facilities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Pre-COVID-19, we were able to enjoy creative offerings by both local and international artists.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As we emerge from COVID-19, I believe we need to redouble our efforts in bringing back arts and culture into our community and not undermine the many aspects of what it can offer, of which I will discuss two.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One: a challenge for society in recent years is that with online and social media, we risk taking out bigotry into the virtual space and echo chambers get formed very quickly.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that arts can offer a safe space for difficult issues to be discussed, but also a space where differences can be better understood.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How precious it is that music from different faiths, traditions and communities can coexist?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This is also very much a part of what it means to be Singaporean – our ability to appreciate and celebrate our diversity.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Two: another challenge coming out of COVID-19 is that the most vulnerable in society as well as our young have had that quality of human interaction greatly diminished.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The arts and cultural spaces are ways for us to safely rebuild that sense of community.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Tough issues, for example, bullying, which is an increasing challenge our young people face today can be more comfortably discussed by kids, parents and teachers when presented in art form.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For the young, in particular, art can help kids open up, offer a way for them to learn about themselves and the world more holistically, to develop empathy, imagination but also an appreciation of Singapore in the world.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Arts and culture have and can play an important part to bolster our fraternity, solidarity and mettle.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: It is an essential part of nation building.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: We are very proud of how far our artists and cultural institutions have come over the years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: We must, therefore, ensure that we do our utmost in continuing to support them in the best way possible.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: The COVID-19 pandemic, as we know, put the hard brakes on the positive development in the arts.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: The cancellation of productions, the drastic drop in tourist numbers and reduced audience size severely affected the arts sector.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: MCCY has been cognisant of this and, in an effort to uplift the sector through the pandemic, introduced the Arts and Culture Resilience Package (ACRP) to protect livelihoods and build capabilities.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I, therefore, invite the Minister to share with this House an update on the impact of the ACRP and the support provided to cultural organisations and self-employed persons.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Given that we are in a much better position now to resume more and more arts and culture activities progressively in line with what the national health situation allows, I also invite the Minister to share MCCY's strategies to revitalise the arts sector as we move forward into the new normal, so as to ensure that our arts groups and practitioners are well-positioned to thrive in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Having adequate funding is a key component for any project or programme to achieve the goals set.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: The arts, culture and heritage sectors are no different.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Beyond Government funding, the private and people sectors are key partners of the arts and culture community.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Philanthropy has, traditionally, been an important source of funding for the arts groups and practitioners.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: The Cultural Matching Fund (CMF) supports the endeavour to attract private cash donations as it provides dollar-for-dollar matching grants to registered charities in the arts, culture and heritage sectors.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Over the years, this has boosted private sector giving significantly and is also well-received by arts groups.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I, therefore, invite the Minister to provide an update on the outcome of the review and to share with us MCCY's strategies to ensure a sustainable arts, culture and heritage ecosystem where Singaporeans can contribute and play a part in.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: The National Arts Council (NAC) and the National Heritage Board (NHB) had previously launched the SG Arts and Heritage Plans which identified the priorities for Singapore's arts and heritage development for 2018 to 2022.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Both Plans set out bold visions to champion and cultivate the appreciation and development of the arts and our heritage.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: We are now at the tail end of both plans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I understand that NAC and NHB have started engagements for the next iterations of both plans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I, therefore, invite the Minister to share with this House an update on the progress of the plans, whether MCCY is of the view that both plans managed to succeed in what they had set out to achieve and an elaboration, if any, on the development of the next five-year plans for these sectors.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: It is, therefore, important as we look ahead that the Government considers the development of the culture and creative economy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: One way that we can do so is to enable our cultural organisations and practitioners to capture new opportunities, such as those in adjacent sectors within the creative economy and those brought about by digital technology.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Seen in these perspectives, I invite the Minister to share MCCY's strategies to bring our arts and culture to new and further heights in the future.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Our heritage plays an important role in understanding who we are as a nation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: It represents a part of our shared history.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: As a multiracial and multicultural society, it is pivotal that we preserve and promote our heritage, as it is a core ingredient in building our national identity and sense of belonging as a people.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: We must, therefore, always remain committed to safeguarding our heritage for future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Hawker culture is part and parcel of the everyday life of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: It is a place where we come together to enjoy a meal together.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: From traditional favourites, such as chicken rice, nasi lemak or mee goreng, to new fusion options, such as chicken chop laksa spaghetti or smoked salmon and lala congee, our hawker food culture has evolved and grown into something that is distinctly Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: And we should all be very proud of it.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I, therefore, invite the Minister to share MCCY's plans to further safeguard and celebrate our shared heritage and how we can continue to engage the community to sustain interest in, and deepen our appreciation for our cultural heritage.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: (In Mandarin):   Arts and culture can help cultivate one's mind, preserve our history and values, and deepen Singapore's influence abroad.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The cultures and arts of different races have their own position and development in Singapore, thereby giving rise to our unique arts and culture.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Arts and culture require human interactions and space for expression.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: With the rapid advancement of digital technology, how do we help these workers use digital platforms to create creative products and enter new markets?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, we cannot underestimate the innovation that the arts and culture sectors spur across the economy.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With wellness and inclusion as key focuses, the arts and culture also offer channels for positive social impact.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They encourage education about Singapore's identity, as well as revitalise our city life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition to short-term support for artists and firms, which comes from both the public and private sectors, policies can also leverage the economic and social impacts of culture in their broader recovery packages and efforts to transform our economy.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With COVID-19, digital presentations have provided a lifeline, allowing audiences a new experience in the consumption of the arts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The digital space has provided both opportunities and challenges for local arts groups as they overcome the safe distancing measures and cross into a digital space that is not limited by physical boundaries.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, there is also a need to reimagine the business models used in the arts and culture sector, so that they are sustainable.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Offering free programmes worked for the short run but the arts also need to be monetised.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Effort needs to be placed on the protection of intellectual property in the digital space.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Manpower planning and growth are also crucial as the arts groups rethink how to increase capabilities to augment the production quality of digital works.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Additionally, talent needs to be boosted through the exploration of new ways of blending digital formats with real-life arts and culture offerings.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Training programmes for freelancers and collaborations with the private sector players are some of the ways to further talent growth to ensure sustained development of the arts and culture sectors.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has had an impact on sports participation on many levels, including the cancelling or scaling down of mass participation events.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Safe distancing measures, as well as concerns about the danger of large clusters forming, have had an impact on sports participation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, there are new developments in sports aimed at coping with the limitations of safe distancing measures.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Capacity constraints in sporting venues and the limitations on the way team sport can be engaged have resulted in innovations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An example of innovative approaches to physical space are emerging, such as the use of small box gyms that offer physical fitness enthusiasts a new and different lease of life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, sports and the communal nature of many sporting activities have a huge role to play in the psycho-social aspects of life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These benefits include cooperation, coping with confidence and shyness issues, dealing with stress and coping with aggression and violence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sports can help curb social isolation and serve as a catharsis or outlet for those dealing with emotional issues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sports also play a critical and important role in bringing Singaporeans together.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sports, whether it is through participation or spectatorship, foster a sense of pride and build a confident nation, through interaction with athletes or sports fan bases.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To paraphrase Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Olympic Games, "The important thing in life is not the triumph, but the fight; the essential thing is not to have won, but to have fought well." So, in this regard, sports can be used to develop an individual's resilience as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can MCCY share its strategies to bring sports participation back into the new normal?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can MCCY also share its strategies to restore and reinvigorate national sports participation, increase access to sports facilities and reintroduce mass sports events in a safe manner?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sports have the ability to reinforce the idea of the importance of equality.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the fourth Paralympics in a row, Singapore's para-athletes have come back with a haul of medals, in spite of the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Athletes, such as Yip Pin Xiu and Paraglider Jessica Goh, have gunned for gold, winning the hearts of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other para-athletes, such as archer Nur Syahidah Alim, cyclists Steve Tee and competition partner Ang Kee Meng, have shown how sports can build an inclusive society through opportunities for talent to shine.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In October last year, it was reported that Yip Pin Xiu will receive $800,000 for the two gold medals she won at the Tokyo Paralympic Games in August 2021.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is, indeed, commendable that sponsors, such as DBS and the Tote Board, have stepped in with the cash awards to help the athletes and reward them for their sacrifice.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The work of the Singapore National Paralympic Council (SNPC), which focuses on enabling our elite para-athletes to participate in major games, such as the ASEAN Para Games, Asian Para Games, Asian Youth Para Games, Commonwealth Games and Paralympic Games, has also been crucial as the SNPC has undertaken collaborations to enable our para-athletes to soar.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important to leverage the international success of these para-athletes to encourage more sports participation at all levels.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, what is MCCY doing to provide more inclusive opportunities through sports?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In sports, "it is not the will to win that matters but the will to prepare to win", according to Paul "Bear" Bryant, the late American football coach.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At some of the major games such as the Southeast Asian Games, Commonwealth Games, Asian Games and Olympic Games, major games preparation is an important ingredient in the athletes' preparation to enhance performance and recovery.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Effort also needs to be placed on minimising the distractions and stress faced by athletes during games time, enabling them to focus on their performance.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is also much behind-the scenes work by organisations, such as Sports Singapore and the Singapore National Olympic Council (SNOC), that have collaborated to prepare for major games to deliver preparation plans, games preparation workshops, performance analysis.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Enhanced sports medicine, as well as sports science, are being employed to support athletes in their games preparations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is also the need to invest time and funds in coaching and providing the best in terms of infrastructure, programmes and sports facilities, so that our athletes can thrive stress-free and focused on delivering an optimum performance.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All these preparation and investment are only meaningful and possible if there is psychological support for the athletes and their efforts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What efforts are underway to rally Singaporeans to support Team Singapore?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sports have the potential to galvanise and inspire the nation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: It brought together many Singaporeans from all walks of life to cheer on the Lions.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: For some of us, the matches certainly brought back the fond memories of the Kallang Roar at the old National Stadium.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Many of us who grew up watching Malaysia Cup will fondly remember Fandi, Sundramoorthy and super-sub Steven Tan.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Actually, my family really scream every time Steven Tan comes on.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Those were the days, but Mdm Chairman, the recent Suzuki cup is a good first step to revive our national sports scenes and to reignite interest in sports.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Such sporting events unite Singaporeans and foster a strong sense of pride.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: National sports participation has also been severely disrupted and the facilities bookings limited.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: We would reserve two lanes for differently-abled children and engage a coach from the Bowling Association for Disabled (Singapore) to guide them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Subsequently, Our Tampines Hub also held a once-off beginner cycling session for differently-abled children.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: These programmes were very welcomed by their parents.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: These children require special guidance and there is a lack of suitable programmes for them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: It would be wonderful if they can join their families for cycling or bowling events after this training.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: On the national stage, many Singaporeans also cheered on Yip Pin Xiu and our Paralympic team in the Tokyo Paralympics last year.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Sitoh Yih Pin points out, this crisis of a generation has tested the very core of our resilience as a society.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MCCY and our stakeholders have felt this very keenly.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are a people-oriented, people-focused and community-building Ministry.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Community and camaraderie are the bedrock of cohesion.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This, however, requires the coming together of people, which is something that we have not been able to do quite so easily.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Arts, culture, heritage, religion and sport, to name a few, are critical pieces in our country's path towards development and progress.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They give us our unique sense of identity, instil pride in us as the people of Singapore and foster a collectively stronger, more cohesive community.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are the foundational cornerstones of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The pandemic has underscored just how important those pieces are.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Hence, when Singaporeans interact less, when our young people stop playing sports with one another, when Singaporeans do not come together to enjoy cultural and community events together, the bonds that bind us will gradually weaken.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The long-term effects, if not addressed, may erode our sense of "us" in years to come.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And we will suffer a deficit in social trust.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, in these unprecedentedly difficult times, we will redouble our efforts to replenish and fortify the connections that bring us together.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our arts, heritage and sports sectors are that critical social "glue" that binds us together, instils pride and gives us a warm sense of belonging to our Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To strengthen the threads of our social fabric, we must deepen the partnership among Singaporeans and with the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is the spirit of Singapore Together, where Singaporeans shared their post-COVID-19 aspirations for society during the Emerging Stronger Conversations (ESC) conversations that were concluded last year.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Mark Chay asked about the progress of the ESCs.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have been working with Singaporeans to translate these aspirations into reality.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The ESCs and AfAs were convened in spite of COVID-19, because Singaporeans wanted to come together to rebuild our Singapore together.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will do more to harness this spirit and to work collaboratively with the public.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our arts and culture practitioners were put through a difficult period.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We navigated it, with financial support and targeted support.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But we know that, ultimately, audiences are the life blood of the arts.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Therefore, the resumption of arts and culture activities in a safe manner has been a priority for us.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Over the past year, we have allowed more activities to resume safely as we continued to simplify and streamline safe management measures (SMMs).

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We increased the number of audiences and participants who can enjoy these activities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We simplified SMMs for performers and crew, so that larger productions can be staged, especially international productions, and we provided support to preserve core capabilities and ensure a smooth resumption of activities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Whilst the situation remains dynamic, MCCY and our agencies will continue to advocate on behalf of the arts and culture, and the sports sectors, for a safe reopening.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We remain committed to supporting our sectors through this recovery.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will help support small organisations, as well as lower- to middle-income workers and self-employed persons (SEPs) affected by the COVID-19 restrictions, including those in the arts and culture sector, and the sports sector.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Darryl David, Ms Tin Pei Ling and Mr Sitoh Yih Pin asked about the impact of the $75 million Arts, Culture and Resilience Package (ACRP), which was introduced in April 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The ACRP demonstrated the Government's clear commitment towards supporting the arts, culture and heritage sectors since the pandemic started.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This support was critical, safeguarding jobs and livelihoods, and also protecting talent in the sector.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Of these, 241 organisations were supported under the ACRP Operating Grant, to sustain operations and make for more nimble adjustments in response to the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We understood how SMMs and venue capacity limits weighed painfully on the sector, with lower revenues arising from reduced audiences or visitor capacities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, the re:SOUND collective made use of the VHS to hold a concert, Tapestry with Jeremy Monteiro.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This was held at the Singapore Conference Hall.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Likewise, groups like Pangdemonium and The Singapore Ballet also utilised the VHS.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I was present at Tapestry some weeks ago.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I was present at the Singapore Ballet a few nights ago and I will be present at Pangdemonium's performance this Saturday at the Victoria Theatre.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I hope that Members will also support the arts in the same way.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also used the ACRP to provide opportunities through digitalisation and transformation to meet future challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This allowed the sector to obtain invaluable experience innovating in these new frontiers.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Together with the Capability Development Scheme for the Arts (CDSA), we created close to 15,000 work and training opportunities for the sector in 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On the back of these gains, we took a longer-term view in 2021 – when we understood the pandemic a little more and we understood the sectors a little better.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We wanted to look beyond the pandemic and position the sector for a strong recovery post-COVID-19 and in the mid- to longer-term.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With the second tranche of the ACRP, we supported transformation efforts that encouraged even greater collaboration within the sector to explore opportunities, share best practices and come together to tackle common issues.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: More than 100 transformation projects by over 190 organisations were supported by the Organisation Transformation Grant (OTG).

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Self-employed persons (SEPs) and organisations also came together to develop projects supported by the SEP Grant (SEPG), creating over 5,000 work and training opportunities for our SEPs.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will fully utilise the $75 million for the ACRP by the end of this Financial Year (FY).

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Last year, we incorporated the CDSA and DPG into NAC and NHB's ongoing grants and, this year, we will also incorporate the OTG and SEPG.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Janet Ang asked how we will continue to provide vibrant arts and culture spaces, and about our plans to co-create new models for the sector.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, Mr Darryl David and Mr Sitoh Yih Pin asked about our efforts to revitalise the sector.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We must act proactively to protect and sustain a thriving and innovative arts and culture sector.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If arts and culture become unintended casualties of the pandemic, we will lose a sense of who we are as a nation and what makes us special as a people.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Therefore, we will work with the community to ensure that the sector remains vibrant, innovative, and more importantly, forward-looking, and continues to provide good and meaningful jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That the landscape continues to reflect our shared values, our ethos and our social mores, inspires and uplifts us and forges a strong sense of national identity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our key focus areas are: First, digitalisation as a key enabler for the sector to engage new and existing audiences and complement existing revenue streams.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To encourage more widespread digital adoption, we worked closely with stakeholders and tech partners to develop the Arts and Culture Digital Roadmap which was launched in February this year.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our arts and culture landscape depends heavily on the rich talent of our freelancers.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They are creative and talented and are a source of spontaneity and innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We value them and want to help them to continue to thrive and contribute.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Therefore, we will work with partners to help SEPs build up their skills, improve working conditions, explore new ways for them to create value in the arts sector and also in the wider creative economy.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, developing vibrant and inclusive arts and culture spaces to keep up with the emerging trends and better meet practitioners' needs.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have asked leaders in the arts community to help envision the space and how it can best be operated and managed.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To ensure that 45AS remains a safe space for artistic experimentation, one that supports the work of our young, emerging practitioners and is always inclusive, multidisciplinary as an arts space.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My colleague, Minister of State Low Yen Ling will elaborate further on our focus areas to strengthen the sector.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin asked for an update on the Cultural Matching Fund (CMF).

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The CMF was set up in 2013 to encourage cultural philanthropy, to push arts and heritage charities to also diversify their income streams via fundraising, with dollar-for-dollar matching of private cash donations to arts and heritage charities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This enhances the resilience of our arts and heritage charities, and there has been an encouragingly strong response to this.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To date, a total of 111 arts and heritage charities applied to CMF at least once.
